body.text: The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) has largely become associated with the overall health of the global artificial intelligence ecosystem in recent months, owing to the dominance of its two largest companies, Samsung and SK Hynix. The two semiconductor giants now account for around 50 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI – and the index has become especially vulnerable to industry-related volatility due to their high market capitalizations.

At this stage, it’s important to highlight that artificial intelligence has still been an exceptionally strong tailwind for the KOSPI. Growth related to the technology’s rapid evolution paved the way for the South Korean index to more than double in value since the beginning of 2025. The KOSPI’s six-quarter growth rate between January 2025 and the beginning of July 2026 sat at more than 231 percent.

However, since its June peak, the index has shed more than a third of its value, and there’s been little sign of a recovery. Worryingly, the downturn appears to have been driven by a global slowdown in investor enthusiasm for AI stocks. Fears are growing over the seismic capital expenditures of hyperscalers, which are projected to reach $1 trillion in 2026 alone.

In the United States, investors have also seen an AI slowdown, with the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF slipping 5.39 percent in value since the beginning of the third quarter of 2026.

South Korea unveiled ambitious AI infrastructure plans this summer. President Lee Jae-myung announced plans to commit $880 billion to rejuvenate the economies of areas outside the capital, Seoul. The package will focus on three areas: chip production hubs, data centers, and robotics technology.

But the announcements came in late June. Since then, the KOSPI’s value has slipped by 35 percent – over one-third – although it’s still up 37 percent since the start of 2026. South Korea’s tech outlook appears to be changing at a rapid pace. While memory demand has remained resilient, foreign selling has pushed Korean shares to six-month lows in recent weeks.
The negative sentiment has even spread beyond tech stocks and into domestic automakers and tech stocks, which suggests that the bearish outlook could linger for longer.

This downturn has seen Goldman Sachs cut 25 percent off of its target price for the KOSPI, chopping its 12-month forecast from 12,000 to 9,000 in a note posted in late October. However, Goldman’s chief equity strategist for Asia, Tim Moe, has also provided a timely reminder that the recent sell-offs haven’t made much of a dent in the KOSPI’s long-term growth, maintaining a “strong buy” status on the index.

Even at a lower price target of 9,000, the KOSPI’s implied upside still represents a 60 percent growth rate from current levels. That indicates a clear continuation of South Korea’s artificial intelligence boom period.

At this stage in its development cycle, it’s certainly worth taking stock of the potential gains. Estimates hold that the South Korea AI infrastructure market is set to rally from a value of $2.58 billion in 2025 to $26.75 billion by 2035, representing a CAGR of 26.35 percent. This growth will be driven primarily by the nation’s advanced semiconductor market, as well as AI computing, cloud platforms, AI manufacturing, and the construction of high-performance data centers.

This aptitude for AI growth can help to compound South Korea’s infrastructure initiatives. Developments in the technology can pave the way for new efficiency brought by operational AI agents, which can identify and work toward solutions while identifying bottlenecks in the buildout process.

Critically, South Korea is earning global support for its AI ambitions. Semiconductor giant Nvidia, which is currently the world’s largest company with a market capitalization of $5 trillion, announced plans during the summer to expand South Korea’s sovereign AI factory infrastructure through planned investments that will grow its Nvidia DSX AI factory deployment to 200 megawatts. The move would see the facility at the GAK Sejong data center more than triple its capabilities from an initial 55 megawatts. Collaborators on the project, Naver and Brookfield, are eyeing a 1 gigawatt facility in the future.

The KOSPI remains integral to the scale of South Korea’s AI ambitions. Although the index has shed more than a third of its value since the summer, it’s clear that expectations remain high thanks to its high concentration of semiconductor superstars in Samsung and SK Hynix. With an ambitious $880 billion AI infrastructure buildout already taking shape, it’s important for the KOSPI, as a barometer of the overall health of the AI landscape, to begin displaying some more resilience. But with a strong domestic innovation pipeline, we’re likely to see a symbiotic relationship form as more industry innovations drive investor optimism.

As things stand, South Korea’s AI ambitions aren’t under threat. If the KOSPI can recover to reach new highs of 9,000 over the next year, we might see the nation stake a claim as one of the world’s most important emerging artificial intelligence ecosystems.
